steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on FlaKat, a machine learning framework that predicts the category of flaky tests. Explain why flaky tests are a problem, summarize how they are detected and repaired today, introduce FlaKat and its evaluation metrics, and outline the rest of the paper.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Flaky tests and why they are a problem
2. Existing flaky test detection: dynamic, static, machine learning
3. Repair and the gap between detection and category-specific fixes
4. FlaKat: vectorization, dimensionality reduction, classifier, F1 and FDC
5. Paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Problem
- tests that pass and fail arbitrarily with same software-under-test; common in modern development
- wasted effort in continuous integration, regression testing (industry, open source)
- hinder reliability/validity of research methods: fault localization, mutation testing
- survey of industrial developers: 59% experience at least monthly; 91% deal with them at least a few times a year

2. Detection
- studied since 2009; numerous detection solutions
- traditional: dynamic analysis, repeated test suite executions
- some need hundreds, sometimes thousands, of executions
- order-dependent tests: randomized execution plans, collect results from all attempts
- effective but expensive (computational power, runtime)
- static analysis; machine learning with promising results; ML much faster

3. Repair and gap
- manual repair by category and root cause
- automated repair for certain categories
- gap between detection tools and category-specific fixes

4. FlaKat
- motivated by prior ML work on flaky test detection
- ML approach to predict category of flaky tests
- vectorization: doc2vec, code2vec, tf-idf
- several dimensionality reduction techniques; classifier chosen by F_{1} score and Flakiness Detection Capacity (FDC)
- F_{1}: precision and recall
- FDC: from intrusion detection capacity; information-theoretic
- foundation of author's Master thesis

5. Organization
- Section II methodology, implementation, research questions
- Section III evaluation with F_{1} and FDC
- Section IV related work
- Section V threats to validity
- Section VI conclusion, future directions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Flaky tests are tests that pass and fail arbitrarily with the same software-under-test, and they are common in modern software development. They cause wasted effort during continuous integration and regression testing, which are widely used both in industry and in the open-source community. Failures because of test case flakiness also hurt the reliability and validity of methods proposed by researchers, especially in areas like fault localization and mutation testing. Flaky tests are also encountered often, which makes things worse: in a survey of industrial developers, 59% of respondents said they experience them at least monthly, and 91% of the developers said they deal with flaky tests at least a few times a year.

Researchers have been studying flaky tests since 2009 and have developed many solutions for detecting them. Traditional approaches usually use dynamic analysis, which runs the test suites again and again. Some flaky tests need hundreds, sometimes thousands, of executions before the failure happens, so they are harder to identify. Other flaky tests may only pass or fail if the test suites are run in a specific order, which needs randomized execution plans and collecting the results of all attempts. These tools are effective at detecting flaky tests but they are also fairly expensive in computational power and runtime. Some flakiness detection tools use static analysis instead, and recent studies also added machine learning tools to detecting test case flakiness with promising results. Machine learning solutions are much faster than the traditional methods at finding flaky tests in test suites.

3. Repair and gap
- manual repair by category and root cause
- automated repair for certain categories
- gap between detection tools and category-specific fixes

4. FlaKat
- motivated by prior ML work on flaky test detection
- ML approach to predict category of flaky tests
- vectorization: doc2vec, code2vec, tf-idf
- several dimensionality reduction techniques; classifier chosen by F_{1} score and Flakiness Detection Capacity (FDC)
- F_{1}: precision and recall
- FDC: from intrusion detection capacity; information-theoretic
- foundation of author's Master thesis

5. Organization
- Section II methodology, implementation, research questions
- Section III evaluation with F_{1} and FDC
- Section IV related work
- Section V threats to validity
- Section VI conclusion, future directions

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Flaky tests are tests that pass and fail arbitrarily with the same software-under-test, and they are common in modern software development. They cause wasted effort during continuous integration and regression testing, which are widely used both in industry and in the open-source community. Failures because of test case flakiness also hurt the reliability and validity of methods proposed by researchers, especially in areas like fault localization and mutation testing. Flaky tests are also encountered often, which makes things worse: in a survey of industrial developers, 59% of respondents said they experience them at least monthly, and 91% of the developers said they deal with flaky tests at least a few times a year.

Researchers have been studying flaky tests since 2009 and have developed many solutions for detecting them. Traditional approaches usually use dynamic analysis, which runs the test suites again and again. Some flaky tests need hundreds, sometimes thousands, of executions before the failure happens, so they are harder to identify. Other flaky tests may only pass or fail if the test suites are run in a specific order, which needs randomized execution plans and collecting the results of all attempts. These tools are effective at detecting flaky tests but they are also fairly expensive in computational power and runtime. Some flakiness detection tools use static analysis instead, and recent studies also added machine learning tools to detecting test case flakiness with promising results. Machine learning solutions are much faster than the traditional methods at finding flaky tests in test suites.

After they are identified, flaky tests can be fixed manually according to their categories and root causes. Recent studies also developed automated solutions to fix certain categories of flaky tests, but there is a gap between the tools for detecting flaky tests and the category-specific fixes. Motivated by prior works that apply machine learning models to flaky test detection, we propose a new framework called FlaKat that uses machine learning to predict the category of flaky tests. We look at how effective three source code vectorization methods are: doc2vec, code2vec, and term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf). We experiment with several dimensionality reduction techniques, and we also choose the machine learning classifier in the framework after carefully evaluating and comparing the options in terms of F_{1} score and a new evaluation metric called Flakiness Detection Capacity (FDC). F_{1} score is a popular and effective indicator of model quality because it reflects both precision and recall. FDC comes from intrusion detection capacity for intrusion detection systems and can measure how well a classifier performs from an information-theoretic point of view. The development of FlaKat was also the basis of the author's Master thesis.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the methodology and implementation details of the FlaKat framework and the research questions we answer. Section III shows the evaluation of the framework with two metrics, F_{1} score and FDC. Section IV covers related work, including studies on flaky tests and their state-of-the-art solutions. Section V discusses threats to the validity of this research. Section VI concludes the paper and points out some future directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Flaky tests, which pass and fail arbitrarily with the same software-under-test, are common phenomena in modern software development. They cause unnecessary wasted effort during continuous integration and regression testing, both of which are widely adopted in industry and the open-source community [1]. In addition, failures due to test case flakiness hinder the reliability and validity of methodologies proposed by researchers, especially in areas such as fault localization [2] and mutation testing [3]. The situation is made worse by how frequently flaky tests are encountered: in a survey of industrial developers, 59% of respondents claimed to experience them at least monthly, and 91% claimed to deal with flaky tests at least a few times a year [4].

Researchers have studied flaky tests since 2009 and developed numerous solutions for flaky test detection [5]. Traditional approaches usually adopt dynamic analysis that executes test suites repeatedly [6]. Certain flaky tests may require hundreds, sometimes thousands, of executions for the failure to occur, which makes them more troublesome to identify [7,8]. Other flaky tests may only pass or fail when the test suites are executed in a specific order, requiring randomized execution plans and the collection of results from all attempts [9,10]. Although effective in detecting flaky tests, these tools are relatively expensive in terms of computational power and runtime. Some flakiness detection tools take a static analysis approach [11,12], and recent studies have also incorporated machine learning into detecting test case flakiness with promising results [13]. Compared to the traditional methods, machine learning solutions are much faster at locating flaky tests in test suites.

Once identified, flaky tests can be repaired manually according to their categories and root causes [4,14]. Recent studies have also developed automated solutions to repair certain categories of flaky tests [15,16], but a gap exists between the tools for flaky test detection and category-specific flaky test fixes. Motivated by prior work applying machine learning models to flaky test detection [7] and [17], we propose a novel framework named FlaKat that adopts a machine learning approach to predict the category of flaky tests. Our work explores the effectiveness of three source code vectorization methods: doc2vec [18], code2vec [19], and term frequency-inverse document frequency (tf-idf) [20]. We experiment with several dimensionality reduction techniques, and the machine learning classifier used in the framework is selected after careful evaluation and comparison in terms of F_{1} score and a new evaluation metric named Flakiness Detection Capacity (FDC). F_{1} score is an effective and popular indicator of model quality since it reflects both precision and recall [21]. FDC is derived from intrusion detection capacity for intrusion detection systems [22] and measures the performance of a classifier from the perspective of information-theoretic analysis. The development of FlaKat also served as the foundation of the author's Master thesis [23].

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the methodology and implementation details of the proposed FlaKat framework, as well as the research questions answered. Section III presents the evaluation of the framework via two metrics, F_{1} score and FDC. Section IV discusses related work, including studies on flaky tests and their state-of-the-art solutions. Section V goes through threats to the validity of this research. Section VI concludes the paper and points out some future directions.
